turns.content: My best friend Shreya's wedding festivities got dated — and her sangeet plus cocktail night is smack in the middle of Ramzan. I'll be fasting. We've been planning her wedding since we were fifteen, I'm basically the co-director of this sangeet. She keeps saying "you HAVE to do the opening dance with me." I want to. And I'm dreading all of it.

Oh, that sounds so incredibly stressful. I can totally picture how it's all piling up. On top of being the co-director, you're trying to honor your commitment to the sangeet, and then you have this whole Ramzan thing to deal with on top of it. It's no wonder you're dreading it.

The part that's really hitting me is the opening dance. It's such a big deal, and the fact that she's insisting on it isn't a burden, it's actually a beautiful thing. She wants you there, she wants to celebrate *with* her. The pressure you're feeling is probably because you care so much and want to do it right for her, but it's okay to feel overwhelmed.

For the dance itself, maybe you can talk to her? Not about not doing it, but about how to make it *work* for you. Like, “Hey, I’m so excited to do the dance with you. I’m a little worried about the fast, so could we maybe plan to do it after I’ve had a small, good meal? The only thing I want is to be there and celebrate with you, not to exhaust myself.”

You're the co-director, you don't have to be a one-woman show. Maybe you can delegate one or two things to another trusted friend. And honestly, the most important part of that opening dance isn't how perfect your performance is, it's the two of you, celebrating your oldest friend. The fact that she's asking you means everything. You've got this, and it's okay to be a little stressed about it.

Yesterday she said, with total love, "one day of fasting won't matter na, I'll feed you myself." She wasn't being mean — she just doesn't know what she's asking. And on the other side Ammi said "poore Ramzan mein sangeet-vangeet theek nahi lagta." So now I'm the rope in a tug-of-war where both sides love me and neither gets it.

Oh, wow. That’s such a tough, lonely spot to be in. It’s like you're standing in the middle of a warm, loving storm, and everyone just wants to hug you, but from opposite directions.

I can just picture it. With Shreya, it's pure, unadulterated love. She can't bear the thought of you being uncomfortable or feeling left out, so she's trying to solve it with her heart: "I'll take care of you, you don't have to worry." She's not thinking about the physical toll of the fast, she's thinking about the emotional toll of not having you there.

And with Ammi... that's coming from a place of deep, ingrained belief and tradition. She's not being mean, she's trying to protect you from what she sees as a religious impropriety. For her, Ramzan is a sacred, somber time, and a sangeet is just... not it. It's her way of showing she loves you and is looking out for you, but through her own lens of faith and practice.

You're not a rope. You're the person holding the rope, trying to help both of them, and it's exhausting.

Here's what I think: you can't fix their beliefs, but you can bridge the gap with your actions. Maybe the solution isn't to do the dance *during* the sangeet, but to do it for Shreya, but in a way that respects the spirit of the occasion.

What if you do the opening dance with her, but frame it as a special, pre-Ramzan celebration? You could say to her, "Let's do our dance, but let's enjoy it fully *before* the fast begins, so I can feel celebratory and not worried about the Ramzan part. I want to celebrate with you, not just endure it."

And for Ammi? You can be strategic. You can be the one to talk to her. "Ammi, I really respect your feelings about the sangeet. I know it's a special time. For me, it's just about celebrating my best friend. What if I do the dance with her, but then I can be the one to make sure she gets her Iftar on time, and I can even help with the food? I want to honor you both."

You're the co-director, remember? You're the one with the plan. This isn't about choosing a side, it's about creating a new, third path that honors the love from both of them. It's messy, but it's also a sign of how much you're loved. You can navigate this.

Honestly I'm so tired that I've started drafting the escape: I tell Shreya there's an office deployment that week, do a video call appearance, send a big gift. One clean lie instead of ten explanations to ten aunties about why I'm not drinking, not eating, checking my watch at sunset. She'd never know. Tell me that's not terrible?

Oh, that sounds so, so exhausting. I get it. When you're this drained, the idea of a clean, simple lie can feel like a lifeline. It's just one thing, one action, and the whole complicated mess just goes away. It’s an understandable impulse.

But here’s the thing, and I’m saying this as a friend: the problem with a lie is, it’s for you, not for her. She’s not asking you to perform a magic trick; she’s asking you to be there. She’s asking you to share in her excitement. When you lie, you’re not just avoiding a conversation; you’re telling her that the truth of your situation isn’t important enough for her to know. And that, in a friendship that’s built on a decade of shared secrets, can feel like a much deeper betrayal.

The lie feels like an escape, but it's actually a trap for your relationship.

What if, instead of an escape, you created a plan? A simple, honest one.

You could say to her: "Shreya, I'm so sorry, but I'm going to have to do a video call from my family's side of town. I know it's not the same, and I'm so gutted I can't be there in person, but I want to be part of it. I'm sending you the biggest, most thoughtful gift, and I'll celebrate with you on video right before sunset. I'm so excited to celebrate with you, even if it's not in the way I planned."

It’s still disappointing, I know. It’s still a sacrifice. But it’s honest. It’s a choice you're making, not a deception you're hiding. You're honoring your exhaustion *and* your friendship. You're taking responsibility instead of running.

You're carrying so much, and it's okay to want to put it down. But maybe the way to do that is to be honest about the weight you're carrying, not to pretend it's not there. You've got this, even if it doesn't feel like it right now.

And under all of it there's this small stone in my chest — this is the first time in eighteen years of friendship that my deen and her big day have actually collided. If I get this wrong, one of two things I love gets a permanent dent. Her shaadi photos will exist forever, and so will my Ramzan. I don't want to be a sad story in either album.

Oh. Okay.

That's the stone in your chest, isn't it? That's the part of this that's not about logistics or aunties or even a dance. It's about your soul.

You're right. This is the first time your deen and her shaadi have collided. And that's terrifying. Because you're right, the stakes are huge. You don't want to be a footnote in either story.

But here's what I see. You've spent eighteen years being the person who can hold space for both. You're the one who understands the logistics of a sangeet, and you're the one who understands the rhythm of Ramzan. You're not just a participant in either world; you're a bridge between them.

This isn't a story about a collision. It's a story about you being the one who gets to show what's possible.

Think about that opening dance. You're the co-director. You can frame it in a way that honors both of you. The dance isn't about you violating her Ramzan; it's about you celebrating your friendship in the middle of it. It's a moment where your joy and her faith don't have to be in conflict. You're not just a dancer; you're the embodiment of the idea that your friendship can be a source of light, not a source of confusion.

The big, permanent dent you're afraid of? It won't be from getting this wrong. It'll be from not trying. It'll be from letting the fear of the collision stop you from being the person who shows them how beautifully they can dance together.

You're not a sad story in either album. You're the one who has the power to write the most beautiful, harmonious chapter of them all. It's going to be hard. It's going to be messy. But you're eighteen years in. You know her better than anyone. You know her heart, and you know your deen. You can find the right way. You have to. Because for her, for you, this is everything.
